title.en: The naga king who sheltered the Buddha
title.si: බුදුන් වහන්සේට සෙවන දුන් මුචලින්ද නාරජ

story: Soon after his enlightenment, the Buddha sat in meditation beneath a tree when an unseasonal storm rolled in, bringing seven days of cold wind and rain. The naga king Mucalinda rose from his lake, wrapped his coils seven times around the Buddha and spread his great hood above his head like an umbrella. When the skies cleared, Mucalinda took the form of a young man and bowed. Images of the Buddha seated on coiled serpents beneath a many-headed hood, seen in temples across Sri Lanka, recall this story.
note: A Buddhist scriptural story about a mythical naga, not a description of real cobra behaviour.

title.en: Two naga kings and the jewelled throne
title.si: නාග රජුන් දෙදෙනා සහ මැණික් පුටුව

story: According to the Mahāvaṃsa, Sri Lanka's ancient chronicle, two naga kings, Mahodara and his nephew Cūlodara, were on the brink of war at Nāgadīpa over a gem-studded throne. The Buddha came to the island, preached to both sides about the futility of conflict, and the kings made peace. They offered the throne to the Buddha, who returned it to them, and they enshrined it in a stupa. The story is linked to the Nāgadīpa Vihāra on Nainativu in the Jaffna islands.
note: Here the 'Nagas' are a legendary people of early Lanka, often described as serpent-worshipping, rather than literal snakes.

refs.title: Where two Naga Kings battled it out (Daily FT)
Historic Nagadeepa Viharaya at Nainativu (Amazing Lanka)

story: The Mahāvaṃsa says that Maṇiakkhika, a naga king of Kelaniya and uncle of Cūlodara, was present at the peacemaking on Nāgadīpa and invited the Buddha to visit his own kingdom. Some years later the Buddha came to Kelaniya, the visit remembered at the Kelaniya Raja Maha Vihara near Colombo.
note: A chronicle tradition. The nagas are a legendary people, not snakes.

story: At the entrances of ancient buildings in Anuradhapura and elsewhere stand carved guardstones (muragala). Many show a naga king: a human figure crowned with a cobra's hood, holding a vase of plenty and a flowering branch. The cobra here is a protector, watching over the threshold and everyone who climbs the steps.
note: An artistic and religious tradition rather than a claim about snakes.

story: On the small island of Nainativu, the Nagapooshani Amman Temple honours a serpent goddess, and reverence for cobras runs deep in its traditions. Each year the temple festival draws pilgrims from across the north. Like the Buddhist Nāgadīpa shrine on the same island, it shows how the naga has long been a shared, protective figure in Sri Lanka.
note: Cultural and religious practice, described respectfully. It is not a zoological claim.

title.en: How a village nickname became a scientific name
title.si: ගැමි නමක් විද්‍යාත්මක නාමයක් වූ හැටි
title.ta: ஒரு கிராமப் பெயர் அறிவியல் பெயரான கதை

story: Generations of Sri Lankans have warned children about ඇහැටුල්ලා, the slender green snake said to dart at people's eyes. The name is usually explained as 'eye-plucker'. When European naturalists described the genus in the early 1800s, they borrowed the Sinhala name, and today scientists everywhere call these snakes Ahaetulla. The belief itself has no support: vine snakes hunt lizards and frogs, and their pointed heads simply rest at face height in garden shrubs.
note: The belief is documented folklore. The biology is covered on the species page.

tradition: Rural belief in Sri Lanka and South India

title.en: The rat snake who 'married' a cobra

story: In many villages people say the rat snake is the cobra's husband, and that seeing the two together means a wedding in the snake world. What people usually see is two male rat snakes rearing up and twisting around each other in a 'combat dance' to win territory or a mate. The two species are not related closely enough to pair, and the dancers are usually both male.
note: A popular belief, with the science explained in Myths and facts.
